issues.subcategory: simulated/random data presented as findings
issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that the method and results are based on a randomized Qualtrics-generated dummy dataset rather than observed participant data. Any inferential statistics, effect estimates, hypothesis tests, and substantive conclusions drawn from these data are therefore not empirical evidence and cannot support claims about replication success or failure.
issues.quote:
[IMPORTANT: 
Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.subcategory: abstract draws conclusions from dummy data
issues.description: The abstract reports substantive conclusions despite acknowledging that the dataset was dummy/randomly generated. This is misleading because randomized simulated data cannot provide evidence for or against the identifiable victim effect, deliberative thinking, or the extension hypothesis.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: extension conclusion based on non-empirical data
issues.description: The abstract claims support for the perceived-impact extension even though the results are based on a randomized dummy dataset. This creates a false impression that the extension was empirically supported.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: lack of random assignment/self-selection into conditions
issues.description: The procedures state that participants selected their own intervention and identifiability conditions. Self-selection destroys experimental control and makes causal inference about identifiability or intervention impossible because pre-existing differences between participants may determine both condition choice and donation responses.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: within-subject/between-subject inconsistency
issues.description: The manuscript describes the design as within-subject, but the reported cell sample sizes and ANOVA residual degrees of freedom indicate a between-subjects factorial design. If the study was within-subject, repeated-measures or mixed-effects models would be required; if it was between-subject, the design description is incorrect. This ambiguity undermines reproducibility and validity of the statistical analysis.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively.

issues.subcategory: wrong model if design is within-subject
issues.description: The analyses use ordinary two-way ANOVA with residual df = 994, treating observations as independent. This is inappropriate for a within-subject design because repeated observations from the same participant are correlated and require a repeated-measures ANOVA or mixed model with participant-level random effects.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.subcategory: direction of main finding misreported
issues.description: The text reports that statistical-victim participants donated more than identifiable-victim participants, but Table 7 implies the opposite marginal means: identifiable victim approximately 2.54 and statistical victim approximately 2.25. This reverses the interpretation of the key identifiable-victim effect.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: hypothetical instead of real donation
issues.description: The original studies used real money that participants could actually donate. The replication replaces this with an imaginary donation decision. Hypothetical donations can differ substantially from costly behavior because there are no financial consequences, increasing social desirability and weakening construct validity as a replication of actual charitable giving.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: removal of endowment/windfall procedure
issues.description: The original procedure gave participants $5 from a prior task, which created a concrete endowment and an actual opportunity cost. Removing this procedure changes the psychological context of the donation decision and may change donation behavior independently of the identifiable-victim manipulation.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey  Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.subcategory: combining separate original studies into one altered design
issues.description: The manuscript merges Studies 1 and 3 into a single 2 x 3 design and adds an explicit-intervention manipulation to the joint condition. This is not a straightforward replication of either original study and introduces new cells and comparisons that alter the interpretation of the original effects.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect

issues.subcategory: new intervention applied to joint condition
issues.description: Applying the explicit intervention to the joint condition creates a condition that was not in the original studies and confounds explicit debiasing with the implicit joint-presentation manipulation. This makes it difficult to attribute effects to either mechanism.
issues.quote: The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.subcategory: misclassification as close/very-close replication
issues.description: The manuscript classifies the study as a close to very close replication despite major deviations in donation consequentiality, setting, population, stimuli, procedure, and design. These deviations are likely to affect the target effect, so the study is better characterized as a substantially modified or conceptual replication.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.subcategory: DV operationalization changed
issues.description: The manuscript itself acknowledges that the dependent-variable stimuli are different, including imaginary donation and altered affect measures. This directly contradicts the claim of a close-to-very-close replication because the primary outcome is not operationalized in the same way as in the original study.
issues.quote: DV stimuli | Different | Question adjustment ... Imaginary donation ... Feelings variables measurement

issues.subcategory: sample characteristics unspecified
issues.description: The sample's geographic origin and compensation are not specified, although both may affect charitable giving, familiarity with Save the Children, income, cultural norms, and MTurk motivation. Without these details, external validity and replicability cannot be evaluated.
issues.quote: Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified

issues.subcategory: unrealistic/generated demographics
issues.description: The reported sample has an implausibly old mean age and a range up to 120, consistent with artificial data rather than a real MTurk sample. These demographics cannot be used to characterize the intended participant population or support generalization.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.subcategory: population change from original study
issues.description: The original sample was recruited in a university student center, whereas the replication plans to use MTurk workers. This change may affect donation behavior, attention, socioeconomic context, familiarity with online tasks, and demand sensitivity. It is a substantial contextual difference that should be justified and analyzed.
issues.quote: MTurk workers as participants We will recruit participants on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study recruited participants sitting inside the school centre of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.subcategory: ambiguous preregistration timing
issues.description: The manuscript states that data collection began at the start of the study period and also states that data collection was completed before analyses, while elsewhere saying results will be updated after data collection. This creates ambiguity about whether preregistration occurred before any data were collected or analyzed, which is essential for preregistered confirmatory claims.
issues.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period.

issues.subcategory: contradictory data-collection status
issues.description: The manuscript simultaneously describes the results as based on randomized dummy data and claims that data collection was completed before analyses. These statements are inconsistent and make it impossible to determine whether the reported analyses are preregistered confirmatory analyses, simulated placeholders, or analyses of real data.
issues.quote: All measures and manipulations conducted for this investigation are reported, and data collection was completed before analyses.

issues.subcategory: insufficient procedure details in manuscript
issues.description: The methods section does not provide the actual sequence, instructions, manipulation text, measurement items, response scales, randomization method, attention-check wording, or exclusion implementation. Referring readers to supplementary materials and links is not enough for a self-contained, reproducible methods section.
issues.quote: The session of “Procedure” in the supplementary summarizes the procedure of the current replication study. For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below

issues.subcategory: unclear exclusion criteria and exclusions
issues.description: The manuscript says participants with prior knowledge and failed attention checks were excluded, but does not report the wording of the prior-knowledge question, the attention check, the timing of exclusions, or the number excluded. Exclusions can materially alter results and must be transparent.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: condition-choice instruction creates demand and confounding
issues.description: Allowing participants to select preferred intervention and identifiability conditions may reveal the study structure and create demand characteristics. It also means the intervention factor may reflect participant preference for learning about the effect rather than an experimentally induced deliberative mindset.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: inappropriate main-effect test for identifiability
issues.description: The replication tests identifiability as a three-level factor including a joint identifiable-plus-statistical condition. This is not the same as the original identifiable-versus-statistical contrast and makes the main effect difficult to interpret because the joint condition differs on multiple dimensions.
issues.quote: Replication | a. effect of identifiability on donation (with joint condition)

issues.subcategory: planned contrast does not match hypothesis
issues.description: The contrast compares the identifiable/no-intervention cell against a pooled average of five heterogeneous conditions. This does not directly test whether explicit learning reduces donation to identifiable victims, whether it leaves statistical-victim donation unchanged, or whether the joint condition debiases donation. Pooling heterogeneous cells can mask or create effects.
issues.quote: contrast the mean difference of identifiable/no intervention on donation with the combination of 5 conditions  (statistical/no intervention, statistical/intervention, identifiable/intervention, joint/intervention, joint/no intervention)

issues.subcategory: failure to test simple effects for interaction hypotheses
issues.description: Hypotheses 3 and 4 are interaction/simple-effect hypotheses, but the analysis relies primarily on omnibus ANOVA and a broad pooled contrast. The appropriate analyses would be planned simple effects or interaction contrasts comparing identifiable/no-intervention versus identifiable/intervention, statistical/no-intervention versus statistical/intervention, and identifiable/no-intervention versus joint/no-intervention.
issues.quote: Explicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donation to an identifiable victim but not to statistical victims

issues.subcategory: multiple testing without familywise control
issues.description: The manuscript conducts many ANOVAs and post-hoc tests across donation, aggregated feelings, six segregated feelings, perceived impact, and six correlations. Only selected post-hoc tests use Bonferroni correction. Without controlling the overall familywise error rate or false discovery rate, nominally significant findings such as p = .045 are likely to include false positives.
issues.quote: We conducted a  2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on segregated affective reactions

issues.subcategory: bounded discrete donation outcome analyzed as continuous without justification
issues.description: Donation is bounded from $0 to $5 and may be discrete or ordinal. Treating it with standard ANOVA assumes approximately normally distributed residuals and homoscedasticity. The original study also used ordered probit, but the replication omits it without justification or assumption checks.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression | a. effect of identifiability on donation | This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: assumptions not checked or reported
issues.description: The manuscript does not report checking ANOVA assumptions such as independence, normality of residuals, homogeneity of variance, or influential observations. This matters especially for bounded donation amounts and Likert-type feeling ratings.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.subcategory: effect-size calculation appears mislabeled or incorrect
issues.description: The reported post-hoc effect sizes labeled d appear inconsistent with the t statistics and sample sizes; for example, t = -2.40 with df = 994 would not usually correspond to Cohen's d = 0.076 for a two-group comparison with these cell sizes. Miscomputed or mislabeled effect sizes distort the interpretation of replication magnitude.

issues.subcategory: effect-size confidence intervals inconsistent with significance claims
issues.description: Several reported confidence intervals for effect sizes include 0 even when the corresponding p value is reported as significant, but this inconsistency is not explained. This may reflect rounding, incorrect CI computation, or use of a different estimand, all of which reduce confidence in the analyses.

issues.subcategory: overreliance on p-values despite negligible effects
issues.description: The manuscript treats statistically significant omnibus tests as supported findings even when partial eta squared values are extremely small, such as .007 and .008. With N = 1000, tiny effects can become statistically significant but may be practically negligible and far smaller than the original effect.
issues.quote: Results from Table 9 showed that no significant effect was found on intervention but the identifiability and the interaction effect of identifiability and intervention was supported.

issues.subcategory: replication-evaluation framework not actually applied
issues.description: The manuscript states that replication effects will be evaluated against the original effect using LeBel criteria, but the results section does not apply the taxonomy to classify the replication outcome. This weakens the stated inferential framework for determining replication success or failure.
issues.quote: We aim to study the effect of deliberative thinking on identifiable victim effect by comparing the replication effect with the original effect (d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.11, 0.84]) obtained from the power analysis using the criteria set by Lebel, Vanpaemel, Cheung, and Campbell (2019)

issues.subcategory: unclear and incomplete power analysis
issues.description: The manuscript says the sample size was determined by power analysis but does not report the target effect size, alpha, desired power, planned analysis, allocation ratio, or resulting minimum sample size in the manuscript. This prevents assessment of whether the study is adequately powered for main effects, interactions, and extension analyses.
issues.quote: The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary

issues.subcategory: power based on original possibly inflated effects
issues.description: The planned sample appears to be powered using original-study effects, which may be inflated because the original sample was small and significant. For replication, powering only for the original point estimate can produce inadequate power for more realistic smaller effects.
issues.quote: The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study.

issues.subcategory: no manipulation check for deliberative thinking
issues.description: The central causal mechanism is that learning about the identifiable-victim effect induces deliberative or analytical reasoning, but the manuscript does not report any manipulation check assessing whether participants read, understood, or engaged in more analytical reasoning. Without this, null or positive effects cannot be attributed to success or failure of the deliberation manipulation.
issues.quote: Learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces people’s donation tendency

issues.subcategory: no validation of updated victim stimuli
issues.description: The replication changes the victim information to updated material from Save the Children, but there is no evidence that the new stimuli are equivalent to the original in severity, vividness, emotionality, credibility, identifiability, or perceived need. Stimulus differences could drive donation differences.
issues.quote: We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago.

issues.subcategory: ambiguous donation target in joint condition
issues.description: The joint condition appears to present both identifiable and statistical victim information, but it is unclear whether participants donate to the identifiable victim, the statistical victims, both, or a general charity fund. This ambiguity undermines interpretation of the implicit debiasing effect.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s)

issues.subcategory: aggregation of heterogeneous feelings without reliability evidence
issues.description: The manuscript aggregates diverse constructs such as being upset, being touched, sympathy, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and possibly perceived impact. These are not interchangeable affective feelings, and no reliability, dimensionality, or scoring procedure is reported. Aggregating them may obscure theoretically meaningful differences.
issues.quote: Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.subcategory: perceived impact treated inconsistently
issues.description: Perceived impact is described as an extension variable but is also listed among segregated feelings. This conflates cognitive efficacy judgments with affective reactions and makes the measurement model unclear.
issues.quote: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.subcategory: extension rationale not matched to analysis
issues.description: The introduction frames perceived impact as a mechanism linking identifiability to donation, but the analysis only tests mean differences across conditions. It does not test whether perceived impact predicts donation or mediates the identifiable-victim effect, so the extension does not address the proposed theoretical linkage.
issues.quote: This highlights the importance of how the perceived impact of donation is linked with the identifiable victim effect in this replication.

issues.subcategory: correlation interpreted as prediction despite post-donation measurement
issues.description: The manuscript says affective feelings predict donation, but feelings are measured after the donation decision. A post-decision correlation cannot establish prediction or causal influence because donation may affect reported feelings or both may be shaped by demand characteristics.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.subcategory: post-decision affect measurement vulnerable to rationalization
issues.description: The original and replication procedures measure affective and cognitive reactions after the donation decision. Post-decision reports can be contaminated by justification or consistency motives, limiting their validity as measures of emotions that caused donation behavior.
issues.quote: After the donation, they had to fill up a questionnaire for different cognitive evaluations they experienced which may influence their choice of donation.

issues.subcategory: extension result contradicts stated hypothesis
issues.description: Hypothesis 6 predicts higher perceived impact for identifiable victims than statistical victims. The reported significant post-hoc result instead compares statistical versus joint conditions and reports higher perceived impact for statistical victims than joint victims, which does not support the stated extension hypothesis.
issues.quote: This suggested that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=3.12, SD=1.43) had a higher rating of perceived impact of their donation to help the victims than they faced an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics (M=2.85, SD=1.34).

issues.subcategory: abstract contradicts results on perceived impact
issues.description: The abstract claims that people have lower perceived impact for identifiable victims or identifiable victims with statistics, but the results only show a significant statistical-versus-joint difference and no significant identifiable-versus-statistical or identifiable-versus-joint differences. This overstates and misstates the extension finding.

issues.subcategory: correlation analyses not corrected for multiple conditions
issues.description: The manuscript conducts six separate correlations between aggregated feelings and donation without adjustment for multiple testing. This inflates Type I error and makes any isolated significant result difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: correlation between aggregated feelings and donation across six different conditions (statistical/intervention, statistical/no intervention, identifiable/intervention, identifiable/no intervention, joint/intervention, joint/no intervention)

issues.subcategory: original comparison statistics incompletely reported
issues.description: The original study p values and standard deviations are often marked unavailable, yet the manuscript compares replication and original results. Incomplete original reporting limits the accuracy of reconstructed effect sizes, confidence intervals, and replication-evaluation claims.
issues.quote: Statistical victim | 1.14 | N/A | 2 | N/A | 5.67 | <.01** | .07

issues.subcategory: questionable conversion of original effects to Cohen's d
issues.description: The manuscript reports Cohen's d for original ANOVA main and interaction effects, including an interaction effect, but does not explain the conversion method. Converting factorial ANOVA effects, especially interactions, to d is not straightforward and can be misleading if not clearly specified.
issues.quote: The interaction effect was d = 0.41, 95% CI [0.05, 0.77] when explicit learning was adopted to debias the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: joint condition is not a pure identifiability level
issues.description: The joint condition changes more than identifiability: it presents both an identifiable victim and victim statistics, potentially changes the number of targets, enables direct comparison, and may alter perceived scope and impact. Treating it as a third level of identifiability confounds several constructs.
issues.quote: The third group was considered as a joint condition provided with both statistical and identifiable victim information.

issues.subcategory: implicit learning construct unclear
issues.description: The manuscript describes joint presentation as implicitly learning about the identifiable-victim effect, but participants are not necessarily learning the effect; they are exposed to additional statistical information. The manipulation may induce comparison, scope sensitivity, dilution, or skepticism rather than analytical reasoning.
issues.quote: participants implicitly learning about the effect would not be presented with such information but with the provision of victim statistics in the identifiable victim condition.

issues.subcategory: software and reproducibility details insufficient
issues.description: The manuscript names JAMOVI and R but does not report software versions, packages, functions, or code provenance in the manuscript. This limits computational reproducibility, especially for confidence intervals for ANOVA effect sizes.
issues.quote: We conducted the data analysis with JAMOVI for statistical testing and R for calculation of 95%CI given that such function is not available for ANOVA testing in JAMOVI.

issues.subcategory: tables contain duplicated/inconsistent sample columns
issues.description: Table 4 contains duplicated replication columns and repeated sample-size entries, making it unclear what sample is being described. Such reporting errors reduce confidence in data handling and manuscript accuracy.
issues.quote: Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.subcategory: compensation not specified
issues.description: Participant compensation is listed as not specified. Compensation can affect MTurk participation, attention, attrition, and perceived fairness, and is essential for evaluating data quality and ethical adequacy.
issues.quote: Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified

issues.subcategory: reliance on non-archival cloud links
issues.description: Some project files are hosted on Dropbox or Google Docs and some links are placeholders. Non-archival links may break or change, limiting long-term reproducibility and reviewability.
issues.quote:
Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here>
Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>

issues.subcategory: claim that all measures are reported conflicts with missing details
issues.description: The manuscript claims all measures and manipulations are reported, but the main text omits item wording, scales, attention checks, manipulation text, and exclusion details. This discrepancy undermines transparency.
issues.quote: All measures and manipulations conducted for this investigation are reported

issues.subcategory: causal language despite design and measurement limitations
issues.description: The hypotheses and results repeatedly use causal language such as 'reduces' and 'elicits,' but the described procedure involves self-selection into conditions and post-decision self-reports. Without random assignment and validated manipulations, such causal claims are not warranted.
issues.quote: An identifiable victim elicits more affective feelings than an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics and statistical victims

issues.subcategory: intervention may induce demand rather than deliberation
issues.description: Explicitly teaching participants about the identifiable-victim effect may signal the desired response and induce demand characteristics or reactance rather than purely increasing analytical reasoning. The manuscript treats it as a deliberative-thinking manipulation without addressing this alternative explanation.
issues.quote: participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims.

issues.subcategory: Bonferroni post-hoc criteria inconsistently described
issues.description: The manuscript says Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons are conducted only if effects of identifiability and intervention are significant, but later performs post-hoc tests for perceived impact after only the identifiability effect is significant and no intervention effect is significant. The decision rule is unclear and inconsistently applied.
issues.quote: Bonferroni -adjusted pairwise comparisons  (Note: We conduct the test  only if the effect of identifiability and intervention are significant)

issues.subcategory: significant interaction not decomposed
issues.description: The donation ANOVA reports a significant identifiability-by-intervention interaction, but the results do not provide the appropriate simple effects or cell comparisons needed to interpret the interaction pattern. The broad pooled contrast is not sufficient to explain the interaction.

issues.subcategory: unclear response scales for feeling variables
issues.description: The manuscript reports means for aggregated feelings and individual feelings but does not specify the response scale anchors or whether all items used the same scale. Without this, the magnitude and comparability of feeling scores are uninterpretable.
issues.quote:
Table 8

Descriptive statistics for aggregated feelings across conditions

issues.subcategory: main identifiable-victim hypothesis not aligned with meta-analytic context
issues.description: The introduction notes that the meta-analytic effect size is very small, but the study still frames the effect as a classic robust phenomenon and powers/evaluates against larger original effects. This may bias expectations and interpretation toward the original effect rather than the broader evidence base.
issues.quote: Although the overall mean effect size was only 0.05, the significance of the identifiable victim effect is still crucial
